objectives: Hear /sh/ in initial and final positions of familiar words.
Recognise sh as a two-letter grapheme representing one phoneme.
Distinguish /sh/ from /s/ and /h/ without adding an extra vowel.
Match ship, shop, fish and dish to their sound pattern.
concepts: A digraph uses two letters to represent one phoneme.
In common early words, sh can appear at the beginning or end.
The phoneme /sh/ is one continuous unvoiced sound, not two separate sounds /s/ plus /h/.

definitions.definition: Two letters working together to represent one phoneme.
The smallest sound unit that can distinguish words.
A letter or group of letters used to represent a sound.

workedExamples.solution: The first sound is /sh/, represented by sh.
The final sound is /sh/, represented by sh.
The initial sound changes from /s/ to /sh/.

commonMistakes: Saying /s/ and /h/ as two separate sounds in sh.
Calling every word that begins with s a sh-word.
Ignoring the last sound when listening to fish or dish.
keyTakeaways: sh is two letters but one sound.
Listen for /sh/ at the beginning and end of a word.
Compare ship with sip and fish with fit.
Say the word naturally, then identify the target sound.
